name: Mazur-Mottola Gravastar
description: A star with no horizon and no singularity that passes for a black hole from outside, proposed by Pawel Mazur and Emil Mottola in 2001. A ball of de Sitter space, a vacuum with $p = -\rho$, fills the inside of a thin shell at $R > r_s$, and Schwarzschild's vacuum lies outside it, the three layers Matt Visser and David Wiltshire reduced it to.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: What if a collapsing star never makes a horizon? A black hole of one solar mass carries an entropy of about $10^{77}k_B$, "far in excess of a typical stellar progenitor with a comparable mass" [mazur2004]. Pawel Mazur and Emil Mottola counted that excess among the paradoxes of the classical horizon, and proposed a new final state of gravitational collapse [mazur2004]. A vacuum with $p = -\rho$, the equation of state of a cosmological constant, was Erast Gliner's candidate of 1966 for the end of a collapse [gliner1966, mazur2004]. By 2001 George Chapline, Evan Hohlfeld, Robert Laughlin, and David Santiago had proposed that the horizon is "a quantum phase transition of the vacuum of space-time analogous to the liquid-vapor critical point of a bose fluid", with a metric inside that "may be de Sitter space" [chapline2001].¶Mazur and Mottola built the star in a preprint of September 2001, which reached print in 2004 [mazur2001, mazur2004]. A ball of de Sitter space with $p = -\rho$ sits inside, Schwarzschild's vacuum outside, and between them, where the horizon would be, a thin shell of fluid with $p = \rho$, the stiffest that causality allows [mazur2004]. Their solution "has no singularities, no event horizons, and a global time" [mazur2004]. For a star of one solar mass the shell is about $3 \times 10^{-14}$ cm thick, and its entropy is some twenty orders of magnitude below a black hole's [mazur2004]. They named it a gravitational vacuum condensate star, a "grava(c)star" [mazur2004].¶Matt Visser and David Wiltshire counted five layers in that "onion-like construction", two of them shells of no thickness that hold the stiff fluid in [visser2004]. In October 2003 they merged the middle three into one thin shell, which left de Sitter space, a shell, and Schwarzschild [visser2004]. Their three layer star has $-g_{tt} = 1/g_{rr} = 1 - r_s/r$ outside the shell and $1/g_{rr} = 1 - r^2/L^2$, $-g_{tt} = C/g_{rr}$ inside, with $C$ set so that $g_{tt}$ is continuous across the shell [mazur2004, visser2004]. Unless the vacuum inside accounts for all of the mass, the shell has a mass of its own: by Werner Israel's junction conditions its surface density is $\sigma = (c^2/4\pi GR)\left(\sqrt{1 - R^2/L^2} - \sqrt{1 - r_s/R}\right)$, which is zero at $L^2 = R^3/r_s$ [israel1966, visser2004]. Letting the shell move, they found "some physically reasonable equations of state for the transition layer that lead to stability", and they advised keeping the shell a finite distance outside $r_s$, where its stresses are finite [visser2004].¶Could a smooth star do the same job, with no shell? Celine Cattoen, Tristan Faber, and Visser answered in 2005 that no perfect fluid can: a star whose pressure is negative at the centre and zero at the surface needs a crust where the pressure along the radius differs from the pressure across it [cattoen2005]. Those sideways stresses let a gravastar be more compact than Hans Buchdahl's bound for fluid stars, $R > \frac{9}{8}r_s$ [cattoen2005, buchdahl1959]. In 2015 Mazur and Mottola found a gravastar inside Karl Schwarzschild's star of uniform density, a solution of 1916 [mazur2015, schwarzschild1916b]. Squeezed below Buchdahl's bound, the star's pressure diverges on a sphere inside it and is negative within that sphere, and at $R = r_s$ the sphere is the surface and the whole interior has $p = -\rho$ [mazur2015]. They called it "a fully collapsed non-singular state already inherent in and predicted by classical General Relativity" [mazur2015].¶In light a gravastar and a black hole of the same mass look alike: light from the shell arrives with its frequency lowered by $\sqrt{1 - r_s/R}$, which goes to zero as the shell closes on $r_s$ [chirenti2007]. Gravitational waves are another matter, since a struck gravastar rings at its own frequencies, and Cecilia Chirenti and Luciano Rezzolla's tones of 2007 "can be used to discern, beyond dispute, a gravastar from a black hole" [chirenti2007]. Paolo Pani, Emanuele Berti, Vitor Cardoso, Yanbei Chen, and Richard Norte worked the thin shell star through in 2009, and its spectrum came out "completely different from that of a black hole, even in the limit when the surface redshift becomes infinite" [pani2009]. A very compact one rings like a black hole at first, and only later sends out a train of "echoes", waves trapped inside its light ring that leak out a little at a time [cardoso2016prd]. Chirenti and Rezzolla held the ringdown of the first detected merger up to rotating gravastars in 2016, and concluded that "it is not possible to model the measured ringdown of GW150914 as due to a rotating gravastar" [chirenti2016]. The searches of the LIGO and Virgo catalogues of mergers for echoes, the latest with KAGRA, have found none [abbott2021tgr, abbott2025tgr].

related.text: The outside of the gravastar, from the shell out. The shell sits at $R > r_s$, so Schwarzschild's horizon is never reached [visser2004].
The inside of the gravastar, a ball cut from the static patch of de Sitter space and ending at the shell, short of the horizon at $r = L$ [mazur2004].
Schwarzschild's star of uniform density. Squeezed to $R = r_s$ it is a gravastar with $L = r_s$ and $C = 1/4$, as Mazur and Mottola found in 2015 [mazur2015].

Visser's earlier use of a thin shell, two Schwarzschild exteriors joined at a throat. Visser and Wiltshire took the shell's surface density and tension from the same calculation [visser2004, visser1989nuclphysb].
Gliner's vacuum with $p = -\rho$ at the centre of a collapsed star again, there with its horizons kept and no shell [gliner1966].
A black hole with de Sitter space at its core and Schwarzschild far away, whose horizons Hayward let form and evaporate [hayward2006].
A black hole mimicker made of a scalar field, smooth all the way through, with a regular centre and no horizon [liebling2023].
A thin shell of dust with flat space inside and nothing to hold it up, so it falls and makes a black hole [israel1966].

coordinates.name: de Sitter Interior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the gravastar, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the mass measured from far away
Areal radius of the thin shell, $r_s < R < L$
Radius of the de Sitter space the interior is cut from, $L = \sqrt{3/\Lambda}$ with $\Lambda = 8\pi G\rho/c^4$, where $\rho$ is the energy density of the vacuum inside
Constant that makes $g_{tt}$ continuous across the shell, so that one time $t$ serves both sides; $C = 1$ where $L^2 = R^3/r_s$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ inside the shell, with $r$ the areal radius and $t$ the time of the exterior chart, carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{C\,r\left(L + r\right)\left(L - r\right)}{L^4}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{r}{\left(L + r\right)\left(L - r\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(L + r\right)\left(L - r\right)}{L^2}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(L + r\right)\left(L - r\right)\sin^2\theta}{L^2}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Interior Tortoise

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the gravastar, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the mass measured from far away
Areal radius of the thin shell, $r_s < R < L$
Radius of the de Sitter space the interior is cut from, $L = \sqrt{3/\Lambda}$ with $\Lambda = 8\pi G\rho/c^4$, where $\rho$ is the energy density of the vacuum inside
Constant that makes $g_{tt}$ continuous across the shell, so that one time $t$ serves both sides; $C = 1$ where $L^2 = R^3/r_s$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, \theta, \phi)$ inside the shell, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$ the tortoise coordinate, a length, so the areal radius is $r = L\tanh(\sqrt{C}\,x/L)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
